extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in evolutionary biology and quantitative biology
extracted.subtask_description: Quantitative and methodological guidance for detecting, classifying, and measuring forms of sexual selection (preferential/assortative mating and reproductive selection) using statistical samples, correlation/regression, and specific measures of homogamy. Emphasises sampling design, control of confounders, and interpretation of statistical error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of forms of selective mating
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify selective mating into autogamic (self-fertilisation), endogamic (mating within family/brood/clan), homogamic/assortative (like with like), apolegamic/preferential (Darwinian sexual selection—some individuals monopolise mates or some are rejected), heterogamic (mating of unlikes), and pangamic (random mating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories (a to f) in their broadest senses to characterise the mating habit of a form of life; the presence or absence of these forms determines potential for differentiation. (Original terms and explanatory notes are given, e.g., autogamy covers all fertilisation within the individual; apolegamy corresponds to Darwin's narrower sexual selection.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting preferential mating by comparing type and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover whether preferential mating with regard to any organ or character is taking place, investigate whether the type and variability of the mated and unmated members of one or other sex are the same; if they are not, sexual selection in the form of preferential mating is at work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare distributions (means/types and variability) between mated vs unmated groups; a difference indicates preferential mating. Beware that the organ measured may be correlated with the actual preferred organ, so affirmation of preferential mating can be safest without specification of characters. Example: compare 1000 husbands vs 1000 bachelors, or wives vs spinsters, matched for age and class, and measure stature or hair/eye colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure sample homogeneity and appropriate comparison groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Mated and unmated material must be homogeneous (e.g., same age and social class) to avoid confounding by age, growth, or selection acting on offspring; avoid comparing parents and offspring directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose comparison groups from the same period of life and class (e.g., husbands vs bachelors of 45–50 from same class). If homogeneity cannot be achieved, results may reflect other causes. Take precautions that reproduction itself hasn't influenced the quantitative value of the character investigated (childbearing may alter stature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for correlated characters before inferring direct preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume the measured organ is the direct object of preference; the measured character may be modified owing to selection on a correlated organ (eye-colour correlated with hair-colour, complexion, stature, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret differences cautiously; where possible, measure multiple correlated characters and consider multivariate explanations. It is safest to affirm the existence of preferential mating without specifying which character is directly preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ample, ad hoc-collected statistics and quantitative tests rather than argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than relying on debate, collect statistics and obtain quantitative measurements (including probable errors) to determine whether sexual selection is a vera causa of evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect sufficiently large and purpose-designed datasets; compute probable errors to test whether observed differences are significant (differences need to be several times the probable error to be considered significant). Examples in the text show use of 'probable error' ± values for means and variabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and sample size guidance (practical sampling examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design studies with substantial sample sizes (examples: 1000 husbands and 1000 bachelors; 1000 wives and 1000 spinsters) drawn from the same social/age strata to detect preferential or assortative mating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text illustrates how non-ad-hoc small datasets may fail to show effects; larger, purpose-collected samples reduce probable error and allow significant detection. If available, compare mated individuals to the general population of same age/class to see if they form a distinct group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure assortative mating by correlation/regression between mates
rubrics_metrics.description: Form correlation tables (or regression lines) between mates' values for a trait (e.g., stature) to quantify resemblance and thus assortative mating; compute correlation coefficient r and its probable error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regression methods as indicated in prior chapters: e.g., r = 0.2872 ± .0196 for stature between husband and wife. Compare resulting r to expected genetic relatedness values (e.g., uncle-niece, cousins) for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling ordinal/categorical traits: median split and the e/2e/N homogamy measure
rubrics_metrics.description: For characters without a true quantitative scale (e.g., eye-colour grouped into ordered categories), divide individuals at the median into two equal classes and compute the excess e of like-with-like matings over the random expectation. The relative proportion 2e/N measures homogamy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If e = 0 there is random mating; if e = N/2 it is absolute homogamy. The text gives the numerical procedure based on median splitting and counting cross-tabulations (example using 774 husband-wife pairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PM (sine of central angle) as a normalized measure of homogamy related to correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert the proportion e/N into an angular measure (angle POX = e/N of four right angles) and use the sine PM of that angle as the homogamy coefficient ranging 0–1; under normal distributions PM equals the coefficient of correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PM behaves desirably: PM = 0 for random mating, PM = 1 for complete homogamy; for quantitative normally-distributed traits PM equals the usual correlation coefficient. The book provides the geometric/trigonometric rationale and an example (PM = .1002 ± .0378 for eye-colour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach for categorical correlation computation
rubrics_metrics.description: When categories are used instead of continuous measures, apply general methods (e.g., Sheppard's theorem) to derive correlation from grouped data; adapt the contingency/table approach to estimate excess like-with-like matings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method illustrated (median split → e → PM) is described as perfectly general and applicable to all correlation problems, citing W. F. Sheppard. Use appropriate classification into ordered groups and compute expected vs observed counts under pangamy to obtain excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess statistical significance using probable errors and error propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Express estimates (means, variabilities, correlation coefficients, PM) with their probable errors and determine significance by comparing differences to their probable errors; differences should exceed the probable error by multiple times to be meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show differences with ± probable error values; the text notes only one of four stature differences exceeded probable error in an example and thus was not significant. Use probable error as the mathematician's test of probable divergences of true from observed values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for genetic (reproductive) selection by correlating fertility with other characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether fertility (reproductivity) is correlated with other characters by forming correlation tables with fertility as one variable and physical characters as the other; if correlated, reproductive selection can drive progressive change in type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments such as pairing moths and recording fertile eggs, or measuring plant characters and seed yield, or measuring human pelvic/stature measures and family size across fecund periods. Lack of ad hoc material is noted; collecting dedicated fertility-correlated data is essential. The text outlines three outcome cases and their evolutionary consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret evolutionary implications: stability requires alignment of modal type and maximum-fertility character
rubrics_metrics.description: If fertility is correlated with a character, the population will change until the modal type coincides with the character value associated with maximum fertility, or until selective death-rates balance the change; thus determining fertility correlations is crucial for evolutionary inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes three scenarios (character of max fertility outside range, within range but not modal, coinciding with modal) and their dynamical outcomes on type and variability. Use these theoretical outcomes to interpret empirical fertility correlations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate sources of change before synthesis (experimental simplification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Like the physicist, the biologist must first deal with the simplest possible fields: isolate individual sources of change (e.g., isolate sexual selection, reproductive selection) and study them individually before attempting synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological prescription advises simplifying experimental conditions to disentangle causes (e.g., consider fecund periods, control death-rates) so resultant effects can later be combined into a full synthesis.
